title: Fabric Data Warehouse integration with Fabric User Data Functions (Preview)
text: Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse now integrates with Fabric User Data Functions in preview, so you can extend T-SQL with custom Python logic without building separate applications or pipelines. Use the integration to send email or Teams messages, retrieve parameters and secrets from Fabric variable libraries or Azure Key Vault, and access data across OneLake. These capabilities are now available directly from T-SQL queries in your Warehouse. Figure: Calling a Fabric User Data Function from a T-SQL query in Fabric Data Warehouse. You can create T-SQL external functions in Fabric Data Warehouse that reference Python functions in a Fabric User Data Functions item. You can then invoke those functions from familiar statements such as SELECT, INSERT, and UPDATE. When an external function is called, Data Warehouse delegates its execution to the Fabric User Data Functions runtime. This integration enables scenarios such as: Calling Fabric or external APIs and sending email, Teams messages, or notifications. Reading Excel, XML, PDF, and other file formats through Python. Accessing data in OneLake and reading from or writing to Fabric databases, Azure Cosmos DB, and warehouses across workspaces. Retrieving secrets and configuration values from Azure Key Vault or Fabric variable libraries to parameterize custom logic. Encrypting, decrypting, or masking sensitive columns with custom Python logic and organization-managed keys. Enriching and validating data by geocoding addresses, verifying VAT or IBAN numbers, or scoring records with a machine learning model. Example: Use Python to classify IPv6 network events from T-SQL Classifying IPv6 events by network prefix can support security analysis, but the required parsing and binary arithmetic are complex in T-SQL. Python provides a purpose-built standard library for this task, allowing warehouses that store network and security telemetry to organize events into consistent network ranges for analysis. In this example, Python’s ipaddress function accepts an IPv6 address and prefix length and returns the corresponding network in CIDR notation. Persisting this value as an analytics column lets downstream queries group events into consistent network ranges without repeating calculation. import ipaddress import fabric.functions as fn udf = fn.UserDataFunctions() @udf.function() def getIpv6Network(address: str, prefixLength: int) -> str: interface = ipaddress.ip_interface(f"{address}/{prefixLength}") return str(interface.network) The published Python function is mapped to a T-SQL external function that accepts an IPv6 address and prefix length and returns the corresponding network prefix in CIDR notation. CREATE FUNCTION ipv6.get_network AS EXTERNAL FUNCTION utilities.getIpv6Network; You can then calculate and persist a /48 network prefix for each event: UPDATE dbo.NetworkEvents SET NetworkPrefix = ipv6.get_network(SourceIp, 48) WHERE NetworkPrefix IS NULL; Each call to ipv6.get_network delegates execution to the Fabric User Data Function runtime. After the result is stored in NetworkPrefix column, downstream queries can use it without recalculating the prefix. Conclusion Fabric User Data Functions let teams continue working in T-SQL while using Python to address scenarios that traditionally require separate applications or pipelines. Explore the preview and start extending your Fabric Data Warehouse solutions with custom logic today. You learn how to use the User Data Functions in Fabric Data Warehouse in the documentation. Try this feature during the preview and share your feedback with the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit .

title: Retiring the Fabric data agent custom tool in Microsoft Foundry: move to Fabric IQ
text: In March 2025, we announced that agents in Microsoft Foundry could use Fabric data agents to answer questions about data in Microsoft Fabric. In the earlier integration, you connected to a data agent by adding it as a custom tool. For details, refer to Consume a data agent in Microsoft Foundry . What’s changing We are deprecating the earlier custom-connection integration. Starting 11/6, 2026, that integration will no longer be supported. If your Foundry agents use a Fabric data agent as a custom tool, you must migrate them before that date. The replacement integration (Preview) uses the Fabric IQ (OneLake Catalog) tool, which makes your data available to agents and applications. In the Foundry portal, you can use this tool to add a published Fabric data agent to a Foundry agent. For configuration steps, refer to Consume Fabric data agent from Microsoft Foundry via Fabric IQ . Capabilities with the new integration The replacement integration changes how you find and connect Fabric data agents: Select accessible published data agents from the catalog. In the Foundry portal, the OneLake Catalog shows the published data agents available to you by name, so the connection workflow does not require you to enter a workspace ID or an artifact ID. Connect more than one data agent. A Foundry agent can call multiple data agents, such as separate agents for sales data and customer support data. The earlier custom-connection integration only supported one Fabric data agent. Connect through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint. MCP is an open standard for how an agent calls a tool. Each selected Fabric data agent is presented to the Foundry agent as a tool through a MCP endpoint. Coming soon, when a data agent answers a question, its response will also include the query it used to generate the answer. What you need to do If any of your Foundry agents use a Fabric data agent as a custom tool, complete the following steps before 11/6/2026: In Microsoft Fabric, make sure to publish your Fabric data agent with a rich and detailed description. Open the agent in the Microsoft Foundry portal. In the Tools section, add the Fabric IQ (OneLake Catalog) tool, and then select your data agent from the catalog. Update the Foundry agent's instructions. Name each data agent and describe the types of questions it should handle. Remove the earlier custom tool and then save the Foundry agent. Test the Foundry agent with representative questions for each connected data agent. If you connect data agents in code, update your implementation to use the Fabric IQ tool. For samples in Python, C#, and JavaScript, refer to Connect agents to Microsoft Fabric with Fabric IQ . Guides to migrate from Fabric Data Agent to Fabric IQ tool Option 1: Migrate in Foundry Portal Navigate to Foundry Portal and open the Tools Catalog, select “Fabric IQ (OneLake Catalog)”. Figure: Select FabricIQ (OneLake Catalog) from the tools . In the OneLake catalog, filter by “Data agent” type. Figure: Filter by Data Agent in the OneLake Catalog and select data agent. Select any data agent you want to use, and you are ready to go. Provide instructions to your Foundry agent about how to use Fabric data agent. Figure: Add Fabric data agent to your Foundry agent and provide instructions . Option 2: Migrate in SDK/Rest API After you publish the Fabric data agent, open its Settings and go to the Model Context Protocol tab. This tab shows: Data agent MCP server name MCP server URL (copy this value; you can use in every client) Data agent MCP tool name MCP server tool description Figure: Navigate to data agent setting to find the MCP server URL. Once you get the data agent MCP server URL, proceed with the following steps: Step 1: Get an access token az account get-access-token --resource https://management.azure.com --query accessToken -o tsv Step 2: Create a Foundry connection to the Fabric data agent A connection stores the Fabric data agent endpoint and how to sign in to it. Your agent uses this connection to reach Fabric. Replace each value in angle brackets, then run the request: curl --request PUT \ --url 'https://management.azure.com/subscriptions/ /resourceGroups/ /providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/ /projects/ /connections/ ?api-version=2025-04-01-preview' \ --header 'Authorization: Bearer ' \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{ "type": "Microsoft.MachineLearningServices/workspaces/connections", "properties": { "authType": "UserEntraToken", "group": "AzureAI", "category": "RemoteTool", "target": " ", "audience": "https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/.default", "isSharedToAll": true, "sharedUserList": [], "UseCustomConnector": false, "Credentials": { "ClientId": "fake" }, "metadata": { "ApiType": "Azure" } } }' Main field capabilities: Field Value What it means authType UserEntraToken The agent calls Fabric as the signed in user, with that user's Microsoft Entra token. category RemoteTool The connection points to a remote tool, in this case an MCP endpoint. target Your MCP endpoint The address of your Fabric data agent. audience https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/.default The token is issued for the Fabric API. isSharedToAll true Every user in the Foundry project can use the connection. Credentials.ClientId fake Keep this value as shown. The response includes an id field. This is the full resource ID of the connection. Save it for step 4. It looks like this: /subscriptions/ /resourceGroups/ /providers/Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/ /projects/ /connections/ Step 3: Install the Python packages pip install "azure-ai-projects>=2.2.0" azure-identity Step 4: Set the environment variables Variable Where to find it FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT The Overview page of your Foundry project. FOUNDRY_MODEL_NAME The deployment name of your model in your Foundry project. FABRIC_IQ_PROJECT_CONNECTION_ID The full connection resource ID from step 2. Use the full ID, not only the connection name. export FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT=" " export FOUNDRY_MODEL_NAME=" " export FABRIC_IQ_PROJECT_CONNECTION_ID=" " Step 5: Create an agent that uses the Fabric IQ tool and ask it a question This script creates a prompt agent with the Fabric IQ tool, sends it one question, prints the answer, and then deletes the agent. import os from azure.identity import DefaultAzureCredential from azure.ai.projects import AIProjectClient from azure.ai.projects.models import PromptAgentDefinition, FabricIQPreviewTool endpoint = os.environ["FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT"] with ( # Signs in with your Azure command line interface account (from az login). DefaultAzureCredential() as credential, AIProjectClient(endpoint=endpoint, credential=credential) as project_client, project_client.get_openai_client() as openai_client, ): # 1. Define the Fabric IQ tool. It uses the connection you created in step 2. fabric_iq_tool = FabricIQPreviewTool( project_connection_id=os.environ["FABRIC_IQ_PROJECT_CONNECTION_ID"], require_approval="never", # The agent calls the tool without asking you first. ) # 2. Create the agent with your model, its instructions, and the Fabric IQ tool. agent = project_client.agents.create_version( agent_name="MyAgent", definition=PromptAgentDefinition( model=os.environ["FOUNDRY_MODEL_NAME"], instructions="Use the available Fabric IQ tools to answer questions and perform tasks.", tools=[fabric_iq_tool], ), ) print(f"Agent created (id: {agent.id}, name: {agent.name}, version: {agent.version})") # 3. Ask the agent a question. Change this to a question about your own data. user_input = "Which customers placed orders above $10,000 last quarter?" response = openai_client.responses.create( input=user_input, extra_body={"agent_reference": {"name": agent.name, "type": "agent_reference"}}, ) print(f"Agent response: {response.output_text}") # 4. Delete this agent version so unused versions don't build up in your project. project_client.agents.delete_version(agent_name=agent.name, agent_version=agent.version) print("Agent deleted") Finally, run

title: Advanced NL2SQL and advanced DAX generation in Fabric data agents (Generally Available)
text: Data agents in Microsoft Fabric let users ask questions about data in plain language. As a creator, you connect an agent to supported sources—including SQL databases, lakehouses, Power BI semantic models, and eventhouses—add the business context it needs, and share it with users across Fabric, Teams, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio, and Microsoft Foundry. The data agent can then respond like a domain expert that understands what your tables mean, how your metrics are defined, and which source can answer a question. The usefulness of a data agent ultimately depends on a simple question: can it translate what a user asks into the right query? That is harder than it sounds. Enterprise schemas are rarely intuitive. Several tables, columns, measures, or join paths may appear to answer the same question, so a query can be technically valid but still return the wrong result. Advanced NL2SQL and advanced DAX generation help address this problem by allowing the agent to explore the schema and data, validate assumptions, and refine its approach before generating a query. Both capabilities are available today, and we'll begin rolling the core improvements out to the standard runtime on November 2, with the rollout expected to complete by November 10. In this post, we'll look at how they work, what our internal benchmarks show, the new configurations available for shaping how the agent behaves, and what to consider as you re-test and evaluate your data agents. Why conversational analytics gets harder with enterprise data Turning a plain-language question into a correct query is a complicated problem, both for SQL and DAX, requiring the agent to resolve several challenges at once: Schemas are large. Enterprise sources can contain hundreds of tables, columns, and measures, and the names alone may not explain when or how they should be used. Business context exists outside the data. Definitions such as “revenue” or “active customer” often live in documentation, previous queries, or analysts’ knowledge rather than in the source schema. Filter values must match the way data is stored. Users describe concepts naturally, but those concepts must map to the values in the data. For example, a user may ask about “California” when the relevant column stores the value “CA.” Questions are ambiguous. More than one column, calculation, or join may appear to satisfy a request. Individually, each of these can be managed with enough hand-written guidance. The difficulty is that they compound: a single-pass generator has to resolve all of them at once — your schema, your definitions, your filter values — committing to an interpretation before it has any evidence that interpretation is right. When it guesses wrong, the query still runs, and the answer looks no different from a correct one. Advanced NL2SQL and advanced DAX generation are built around that problem. Rather than generating a single pass, the agent gathers evidence first. Advanced NL2SQL: the agent explores before it writes The shift is architectural. Instead of one-shot generation, the agent has sub-tools to explore schema, test joins, and look up real filter values before it writes SQL. Under the hood, you can inspect each step the agent took, and the assumptions and reasoning behind it. It operates in three modes, each backed by its own sub-tools: Mode What it does Example query following Finds a relevant example query and answers by making approved modifications, such as literal filter or parameter substitutions. Clarifying questions Determines it can’t answer reliably without more information and asks targeted clarifying questions before generating SQL. Data exploration When no example directly applies, learns from existing example queries to infer business logic, explores the data to validate assumptions, and iteratively refines its approach. What you get as a creator: Advanced NL2SQL explores the SQL source schema, tests joins, and looks up real filter values before generating SQL, helping it choose the appropriate tables, columns, relationships, and filters. Schema descriptions and topics that teach the agent what your data means, so you get better answers with fewer instructions. Better example-following and filter-value substitution for novel questions. Handles large schemas far better and runs faster end to end, with more reasoning detail for debugging. New configurations: schema descriptions and topics Two new configurations give the agent more of the context it needs. Both are available for SQL data sources on the preview runtime. Schema descriptions Schema descriptions attach business context to the objects in your data source — what a table holds, what a column represents, and how each should be used. The agent uses them to interpret large or ambiguous schemas and generate a more accurate query. They matter most where object names don’t carry meaning on their own, or where several tables and columns look interchangeable. Figure: Schema descriptions add business context to schema objects, helping the data agent interpret your data. Topics Topics help you give the agent detailed guidance without sending every instruction with every question. The agent searches your topic content and uses only the sections relevant to the current request. Use data source instructions for rules that must always apply, and use topics for deeper guidance that applies only to a specific subject. You can write topics in Markdown, import multiple files, and review the run steps to see which topics the agent selected. Figure: Topics organize subject-specific instructions in Markdown to guide the data agent’s query generation. Internal benchmark testing: Advanced NL2SQL on Preview Runtime vs NL2SQL on Standard Runtime Better reasoning matters only if it produces better answers without making users wait substantially longer. In an internal benchmark set evaluating answer quality and end-to-end latency, the preview runtime delivered the stronger outcome, answering more questions correctly than the standard runtime while reducing both median and tail latency. Smart-answer accuracy increased from 78.8% to 90.9%. Latency improved at the same time: P50: 28.4 seconds to 26.0 seconds P95: 46.8 seconds to 32.9 seconds Figure: Smart answer accuracy and end-to-end latency, standard runtime versus the Advanced NL2SQL preview, on an internal benchmark set. Accuracy rises 12.1 points to 90.9%, while P50 latency falls 8.3% and P95 falls 29.8%. *Performance results are based on Microsoft internal testing conducted in 2026 using an internal evaluation set comparing standard NL2SQL to the advanced NL2SQL preview in Microsoft Fabric. Actual results may vary depending on workload, data model, and configuration. The P95 result shows the largest latency improvement in this benchmark, with latency decreasing from 46.8 seconds to 32.9 seconds. This improvement is most relevant to the slower, more complex queries represented at the tail of the distribution. Advanced DAX generation: agentic reasoning over semantic models The agent calls tools, inspects results, and refines its approach to answer harder questions. Instance value indexing searches real column values, so filters match your data. And you get consistent results across Data Agent, Power BI, and M365 Copilot. For users, this means the agent is more likely to resolve filter terms to the values stored in the semantic model and return consistent answers across supported Microsoft experiences. Internal benchmark testing: Advanced DAX generation improves accuracy while cutting latency Our internal Advanced NL2DAX evaluation showed improvements in both answer accuracy and latency. Smart-answer accuracy increased from 89.15% to 91.86% . At the same time: P50 latency: 39.1 seconds to 20.4 seconds P95 latency: 97.5 seconds to 34.7 seconds This represents an approximately 48% reduction in P50 latency and a 64% reduction in P95 latency, along with a 2.7 percentage-point increase in smart-answer accurac

title: Fabric Policies: Granular governance at scale (Preview)
text: As Microsoft Fabric grows across teams, workspaces, and capacities, governance becomes harder to manage with broad tenant-wide switches alone because governance models are not one-size-fits-all. Fabric Policies provide granular controls that can fit your governance model by defining what actions are allowed, to whom and where . The result is governance that scales with your Fabric estate. Teams keep the flexibility they need to work; capacity admins can protect the resources they manage, and central administrators gain consistent controls and visibility across the organization. Fabric Policies help organizations: Match controls to organizational boundaries - Apply organization-wide rules at tenant scope and resource-specific rules at capacity scope. Protect sensitive actions without slowing routine work - Keep approved self-service available while restricting higher-risk actions to the right users and context. Apply consistent guardrails at scale - Manage policies centrally through Policy Sets, Policies Center, auditing, and public APIs. What you can govern Fabric Policies currently provide controls for item creation, external data sharing (coming soon), and selected security-sensitive workspace settings. Control item creation by capacity Capacity admins can set a policy for any Fabric item type in workspaces assigned to their capacity (Power BI item creation is not yet enforced). An admin can allow the Data Engineering security group to create Dataflow Gen2 items in selected data platform workspaces and the AI Builders security group to create Data agent items in selected AI workspaces. Matching requests proceed; requests that do not match a complete Allow rule are blocked. This control supports a gradual Fabric rollout. Organizations can make specific item types available to approved teams and workspaces as their governance requirements are met, rather than enabling every item type everywhere at once. Item creation requires both controls to allow the request: the applicable Fabric item creation setting and the active Item creation policy. Figure: Advanced Item creation policy with separate Allow rules for Dataflow Gen2 and Data agent. Protect security-sensitive workspace settings Fabric admins can protect selected settings without removing broader workspace administration capabilities. An admin can allow the Central IT team to edit Outbound access protection , Inbound access protection , and Apply customer-managed keys (CMK) in sensitive workspaces. Other workspace admins can continue to edit the rest of the settings. The policy refines what existing workspace admins can change; it does not grant the Workspace Admin role. Govern external data sharing (Coming Soon) Fabric admins can support partner collaboration while controlling who can share, which workspaces the data comes from, its sensitivity label, and the recipient email domain. An admin can allow the Finance security group to share items labeled Confidential from Finance workspaces with recipients at CALDOVA.com. Sharing proceeds only when all configured conditions match; other requests are blocked. External sharing can be allowed by either the existing External data sharing tenant setting or a matching and active policy rule. How Policies work On Policy Set creation, an administrative scope is selected, such as the tenant or a capacity. This defines the available policy types and the administrator role required to activate the Policy Set for that scope. Figure: Policy Set overview showing tenant or capacity scope. For each policy, administrators choose Allow all , Block all , or Advanced . Advanced policies use an allow-based model: All conditions within a rule must match. A match on any complete rule allows the action. If no rule matches, the action is blocked. Once the Policy Set is activated, Fabric evaluates its policies whenever a governed action occurs within that scope. Only one Policy Set can be active for a tenant or an individual capacity. Activating a replacement changes which definitions govern that scope. Existing access requirements remain in effect. Policies do not grant Fabric roles, workspace access, or item permissions. A user must first have the access required for the action; the policy then adds a governance decision for that action and context. Fabric Policies are available in preview for supported Fabric capacities and workspaces. Standard Fabric capacity and workspace requirements apply. Get started with Fabric Policies In Admin portal > Tenant settings , enable Policies (Preview) . In a Fabric-capacity-backed workspace, create a Policy Set and choose Tenant or Capacity scope. Configure a policy with Allow all , Block all , or Advanced Allow rules, then review the users, actions, and workspaces covered. Activate the Policy Set as an administrator of the target scope. For capacity scope, select a capacity you administer. Review the related Fabric setting and policy together, then verify the active result in OneLake Catalog > Policies Center . For repeatable deployment across environments or capacities, use Fabric REST APIs to automate Policy Set and policy management at scale. API operations and activation remain subject to the required item permissions and administrator role. Policies best practices and management Design Advanced policies around every allowed scenario. List every user, item type, and workspace combination that must continue to work. Because Advanced policies are allow-based, a request is blocked when no complete rule matches. Align capacity policies with capacity ownership. Item creation policies govern workspaces assigned to the selected capacity. Each capacity can have its own active Policy Set, giving capacity admins control within their resource boundary. Review policy coverage whenever workspaces move between capacities. Use a dedicated management workspace. A Policy Set can be hosted in one supported Fabric-capacity-backed workspace and activated for a different capacity. A dedicated workspace can simplify access, ownership, and lifecycle management across multiple capacities. Separate editing from activation. People with Read , or the workspace Viewer role, can view a Policy Set. People with Read and Write , or a workspace Contributor , Member , or Admin role, can edit it. Activation still requires the administrator role for the target scope: Fabric admin for tenant scope or capacity admin for capacity scope. Validate before broad rollout. Start with representative users and workspaces and review each allowed scenario. Monitor and refine. Use Policies Center to review active policies and the Microsoft 365 Audit Log to follow Policy Set and rule lifecycle operations. Conclusion As Microsoft Fabric adoption scales across teams, workspaces, and capacities, governance must scale with it. Fabric Policies provide the flexibility to apply the right controls in the right contexts while maintaining a consistent governance model across the organization. By combining centralized oversight with granular policy enforcement, organizations can confidently expand their Fabric footprint without sacrificing security or control. Learn more about policies.

title: Databricks ADBC connector for Power BI and Microsoft Fabric (Generally Available)
text: This release is part of the broader ODBC-to-ADBC transition for Power Query connectors described in the Transition from ODBC to ADBC drivers in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric documentation. What’s new Existing connections in your semantic models, dataflows, and paginated reports continue to work unchanged — the migration path is currently opt-in per connection, per workspace, or per tenant. Highlights: Improved security - ADBC drivers incorporate security enhancements, such as memory safety and garbage collection. No changes to existing behavior - This transition moves away from the embedded ODBC drivers that ship with Power BI. It does not change behavior for the ODBC connector when you use a separately installed ODBC driver. Efficient large dataset support - ADBC provides a set of standard interfaces for interacting with Arrow data, which is especially efficient at fetching large datasets with minimal overhead and no serialization or copying. Supported authentication - Databricks ADBC supports OAuth (user), OAuth (M2M / Client Credentials), and Microsoft Entra ID. Connectors covered by this release Connector Previous driver New driver (GA) Databricks Simba Spark ODBC Databricks ADBC Azure Databricks Simba Spark ODBC Databricks ADBC How to try it You can test the ADBC driver now. We suggest you start soon to help ensure the eventual deprecation of ODBC and migration to ADBC runs smoothly. There are three ways to begin validating ADBC, ordered by how much control you want. 1. Opt in per connection using Implementation="2.0" The fastest way to compare ADBC and ODBC for a specific report or dataset. Add the Implementation="2.0" option to the source step in your Power Query expression: Source = Databricks.Catalogs("adb-1234567890.1.azuredatabricks.net", "/sql/1.0/warehouses/ ", [Implementation="2.0"]) Refresh the dataset and compare row counts, column types, and totals against your production baseline. If you want to force a side-by-side comparison against ODBC, use Implementation="1.0" . 2. Override the default for a validation workspace If you want to validate several reports together, a workspace admin can turn ADBC on for a single workspace while the rest of the tenant continues to use the legacy driver. Publish the reports you want to test into that workspace and run your normal refresh schedule. 3. Enable ADBC by default at the tenant level When you’re confident with the results, the tenant admin can enable Users can connect to data sources by using Apache Arrow database connectivity (ADBC) in the Admin portal. New connections across the tenant will use the ADBC driver by default, and Desktop and the service stay aligned on the same driver. What to expect during validation The ADBC driver is designed as a compatibility-preserving replacement for the Simba Spark ODBC driver. Validate your key reports in Desktop before enabling ADBC at the tenant level and report any regressions to adbcmigration@microsoft.com . Explore Transition from ODBC to ADBC drivers in Power BI and Microsoft Fabric for more information. What’s next The Power BI service will move from ODBC to ADBC through the first quarter of 2027. We recommend that you start validating today, so the tenant-level move is a non-event when it lands. We’d love your feedback Try the new Databricks ADBC driver. If anything looks different from what you'd expect — a refresh that fails, a total that changed, a performance regression — send the tenant ID, connector, M expression, and what you observed to adbcmigration@microsoft.com . Get started this week: Read the Databricks connector documentation . Install the latest Power BI Desktop. Pick one production report on Databricks and add Implementation="2.0" to its source step. Compare row counts, column data types, and key totals against your production baseline. Report anything unexpected to adbcmigration@microsoft.com .

title: File Data Ingestion with Materialized Lake Views in Microsoft Fabric (Preview)
text: File data ingestion with materialized lake views (MLVs) in Microsoft Fabric is now available in preview. Instead of building separate ingestion pipelines to move raw files into tables, you can now ingest CSV and Parquet files directly from OneLake into a materialized lake view and make your bronze layer part of the same declarative pipeline as the rest of your medallion architecture. This capability builds on the recent announcement of Materialized Lake Views in Microsoft Fabric (Generally Available) , extending the simplified approach from table-based transformations to raw file ingestion. Why this matters Until now, you had to build and maintain a separate ingestion layer before you could get the benefits of MLVs, which had to start from tables. To get raw files into that first table, you'd reach for a shortcut transformation, a data pipeline, or a notebook load which is a separate step to build and operate before your declarative pipeline could even begin. File data ingestion removes that step. Point a materialized lake view at a folder of files, and Fabric handles the ingestion, materializes the results as a Delta table, and plugs it straight into the same lineage, scheduling, data quality, and monitoring that power the rest of your medallion architecture. One programming model, from raw files to gold. If you've referred to Simplifying Medallion Implementation with Materialized Lake Views , there was a missing link in the first mile: bronze, expressed declaratively. Now we have resolved that. What is file data ingestion? A file-ingesting materialized lake view is defined with a USING OneLake_Files clause instead of an AS SELECT query. You describe the source folder and format, and Fabric materializes it: CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW bronze.raw_orders USING OneLake_Files OPTIONS ( 'format' = 'csv', 'path' = 'abfss://SalesWorkspace@onelake.dfs.fabric.microsoft.com/SalesLake.Lakehouse/Files/orders/', 'header' = 'true' ) TBLPROPERTIES ( 'schema_mode' = 'DYNAMIC', 'refresh_mode' = 'APPEND_ONLY' ); That single statement gives you a queryable, refreshable bronze table. In preview, file data ingestion supports: CSV and Parquet source files. Recursive folder ingestion — files in nested subfolders are picked up automatically. Schema evolution with DYNAMIC mode, or a pinned schema with FIXED mode which gets auto detected during creation. Source traceability — every row carries a __filepath__ column recording that records its source file. CSV parsing supports the header and delimiter options; additional CSV options and further capabilities are on the roadmap. Build a complete medallion — From files to gold Because a file-ingesting view behaves like any other materialized lake view once created, you can layer transformations on top of it and let Fabric orchestrate the whole chain in dependency order: -- Bronze: ingest raw files directly from OneLake CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW bronze.raw_orders USING OneLake_Files OPTIONS ('format' = 'csv', 'path' = 'abfss://…/Files/orders/', 'header' = 'true') TBLPROPERTIES ('schema_mode' = 'DYNAMIC', 'refresh_mode' = 'APPEND_ONLY'); -- Silver: clean and enforce data quality declaratively CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW silver.orders ( CONSTRAINT valid_amount CHECK (amount > 0) ON MISMATCH DROP ) AS SELECT id, customer, CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS amount FROM bronze.raw_orders; -- Gold: aggregate for reporting CREATE MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW gold.daily_sales AS SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total FROM silver.orders GROUP BY customer; Fabric records the dependency from silver.orders → bronze.raw_orders → the source folder and refreshes them in order. When new files land, the change flows through silver to gold — no glue code, no orchestration to maintain. Trace every file through lineage File data ingestion is fully integrated into the materialized lake views lineage experience. The lineage graph starts from the source folder node, which feeds your bronze view and everything downstream: Select the source folder node to see the OneLake path and the files discovered in it. Select the file-ingesting view to inspect its format, schema mode, and refresh mode. Drill into any run to see how many files were processed and rows added — so you can confirm new data was picked up. Pair that with the __filepath__ column to reconcile row counts back to individual source files: SELECT __filepath__, COUNT(*) AS rows FROM bronze.raw_orders GROUP BY __filepath__; Schema on your terms File-ingesting materialized lake views support two schema modes, allowing you to choose between automatic schema evolution and a fixed schema contract: `DYNAMIC` (default): the view schema evolves with your data — new columns are added and dropped columns handled automatically across files and refreshes. Perfect for landing zones where source shape changes over time. `FIXED` : the schema is pinned at creation and drift is rejected — ideal when you need a stable contract for downstream consumers. Refresh and scheduling, handled for you Just like table-based materialized lake views, you don't orchestrate file ingestion from a notebook. Use lineage and scheduled refresh on the lakehouse to run views in dependency order and pick up new files automatically. Need to reprocess an entire folder on demand? A single full refresh does it: REFRESH MATERIALIZED LAKE VIEW bronze.raw_orders FULL; Key benefits Together, these capabilities help simplify file-based ingestion and bring raw files into the same declarative workflow as the rest of your medallion architecture. One declarative model — from raw files to gold, no separate ingestion step to build or operate. Bronze in a single statement — replace bespoke COPY/pipeline/notebook loaders with USING OneLake_Files. End-to-end lineage — trace data from the source folder, through every layer, down to the individual file. Built-in data quality and scheduling — the same governance and orchestration you already rely on for table-based views. Schema flexibility — evolve automatically with DYNAMIC or lock a contract with FIXED. Get started Open a lakehouse in Microsoft Fabric and drop your CSV or Parquet files into Files . Create a file-ingesting materialized lake view with USING OneLake_Files. Build silver and gold views on top, then schedule a refresh from the Materialized lake views → Manage experience. Resources What are materialized lake views in Microsoft Fabric? Spark SQL reference for materialized lake views Manage materialized lake views lineage Tutorial: Build a medallion architecture with materialized lake views Tell us what you think We built file data ingestion to make the first mile of your medallion pipeline as effortless as the rest of it. Try it out on your own CSV and Parquet data and share your feedback on the Fabric Community — we can't wait to see the pipelines you build.

title: Fabric App functions to use secure server-side custom logic (Preview)
text: Fabric App functions is a new capability that allows builders to add secure, server-side logic directly to their Fabric Apps without standing up separate infrastructure. Built on top of Fabric User Data Functions (UDFs), Fabric App functions give developers a simple way to execute business logic, integrate with external services, access protected resources, and keep secrets from the client. Figure: Get started with functions in your Fabric app. What are Fabric App functions? Fabric App functions are TypeScript-based serverless functions that run alongside your Fabric app. They provide a secure backend execution environment for code that should not run in the browser. Functions are packaged and deployed as part of the application experience and can be invoked directly from the application through a typed client. Think of Functions as the custom logic layer for your Fabric App: Execute business rules and complex calculations Access protected data sources Call external APIs Perform orchestration and AI workflows Store and retrieve secrets securely Access downstream resources using the application’s identity via application authentication Application authentication Application authentication means the Fabric app function accesses a downstream resource using the application’s identity rather than impersonating the person currently using the app. The downstream service sees and authorizes the application, not the signed-in user. How the identity flow works The user signs in to the Fabric App, the app calls the function, and the function then calls the downstream service using the application identity. Grant the application only the permissions it needs. Authorize the application at the downstream service. Keep credentials and tokens out of client-side code. Add application-level validation and business logic before accessing data. Secrets management Functions allow builders to securely store and retrieve secrets without exposing them to browsers or application users. Figure: Add and manage secrets for Fabric app functions. Get started with functions Fabric App functions are designed to feel like part of the application, not a separate platform. Key dependency is to install Azure Functions Core Tools version 4 before you get started. npm install --global azure-functions-core-tools@4 Create an app with functions Scaffold a new app, move to the app directory, and initialize its functions project: npm create @microsoft/rayfin@latest -- "my-app" cd my-app npx rayfin functions init The Fabric App functions init command adds the functions project, TypeScript configuration, and a starter function file to the existing app. Build the app with GitHub Copilot The scaffold includes the GitHub Copilot instructions and skills needed to work with the project. Open the project in Visual Studio Code, then describe the app you want to build in GitHub Copilot Chat. For example, use this prompt to build an AI pull request review assistant: Build an app that lets me view all pull requests for the repository , chat with my Azure AI Foundry agent to review pull requests, and post review comments. Use functions with application authentication to connect to Azure AI Foundry and Azure DevOps. GitHub Copilot can generate and update the required files and components. You can also ask the agent to run the app, debug functions locally, and deploy the app. Debug functions You can run functions locally to test your server-side logic before deploying to Fabric. Use the local Azure functions host to invoke functions, inspect errors, and validate your integration. Once validated, deploy the app and functions together. Run the following command to test your functions and deploy your changes. npx rayfin dev npx rayfin up Conclusion If you’ve been waiting for a secure way to connect Fabric Apps to external services, protect secrets, use application authentication, or build AI-powered experiences, Fabric App functions are the missing piece. To learn more, refer to the Fabric Apps documentation.

title: My workspace governance improvements (Generally Available)
text: My workspace governance features , which give administrators governance controls over their users' personal My workspaces, are now generally available. As My workspaces continue to be used for business-critical content, organizations need governance capabilities that scale with their environment. These enhancements give administrators greater flexibility to access, manage, and recover content when needed, while enabling automation that reduces operational overhead and improves consistency across the tenant. These enhanced tenant administrator controls for My workspace are also available in government clouds. What's new Two new admin REST APIs make temporary admin access to a personal workspace fully programmable: Grant Admin Temporary Access : grants a Fabric administrator 24-hour access to a user's My workspace. Remove Admin Temporary Access : revokes that access before the 24-hour window ends. Both can be called by a Fabric administrator or by a service principal. The service principal identity must be enabled for Admin API access in your tenant settings. SPN support and these new APIs allow tenant administrators to automate management of tenant users’ My workspaces contents instead of doing it by hand in the Admin Portal. Reminder: Restoring orphaned My workspaces When a user is hard deleted in Microsoft Entra, their My workspace becomes orphaned and moves to a Deleted state, with contents retained for 30 days . During that window, you can restore it with the Restore Workspace API. Important: new workspace name is required when restoring a former My workspace, and you assign a new admin to own the recovered content. Try the Admin controls and new APIs and let us know what you think in the comment section.
